summary.summary: Portsmouth ended the year with gross debt of £718m (including £56m of PFI) against investments of £230m — net debt £488m — and took no new borrowing at all, running £292m of internal borrowing instead while new money costs over 5%. Its borrowing need (CFR) is £1,010m, so £292m of real borrowing is deferred, not avoided; the council itself notes this needs ongoing monitoring as the need grows. Net treasury costs came in £0.01m under budget.

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth's auditor expects a qualified opinion on 2025/26 accounts, with no going-concern uncertainty expected
news_drafts.lead:
Portsmouth City Council's external auditor expects to issue a qualified opinion on the council's 2025/26 financial statements, meaning it could not fully sign off the accounts. Its Audit Results Report goes to the Governance & Audit & Standards Committee on 12 November.

The report says the audit work is substantially complete. The expected opinion is subject to the remaining procedures listed in Appendix H of the report. The 2024/25 opinion was also qualified. For 2023/24 the auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion, which means it did not give an opinion on the accounts.

The auditor also reports that it has identified no events or conditions casting significant doubt on the council's ability to continue preparing its accounts on a going concern basis, the assumption that the council will keep operating. It does not currently expect to include an emphasis of matter or a material uncertainty reference in its opinion.
news_drafts.paper_title: Portsmouth Audit Results Report 202526 For GAS

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth covered £292m of its borrowing need from its own cash in 2025/26, taking no new loans
news_drafts.lead:
Portsmouth City Council took out no new loans in 2025/26 and instead paid for part of its capital spending (money spent on things that last, such as buildings and roads) from its own cash, according to its treasury management outturn report for the year. Treasury management is how a council borrows, invests spare cash and manages the risks of both. The report goes to Full Council on 13 October.

The council's capital financing requirement, the total it has spent on long-lived assets but not yet paid for, and in effect its underlying need to borrow, stood at £1,010m. Its actual borrowing was £718m. The £292m difference was met by what the paper calls internal borrowing: using the council's own cash and money set aside, which saves interest but uses up the cushion. The report says this was done because external borrowing rates stayed above 5% and would have cost more than using internal funds.

The effect shows in the council's investments. They averaged £281m over the year but stood at £230m on 31 March 2026. The report says the council "continued to maintain an under-borrowed position and no new borrowing was undertaken", adding that the approach "requires ongoing monitoring as the underlying need to borrow increases."

news_drafts.headline: Portsmouth forecasts £1.052m schools grant overspend, with High Needs £524k over budget
news_drafts.lead:
Portsmouth's schools budget is forecast to overspend by £1.052m in 2026-27, according to first-quarter figures for the Schools Forum. The dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) started the year with a carried-forward deficit of £8.014m. Its high needs block, which pays for children with special educational needs and disabilities, is forecast at £40.797m against a £40.273m budget, an overspend of £524k.

The paper attributes this to more pupils than budgeted. There are 30 more full-time-equivalent pupils than the 1,086 budgeted with education, health and care plans (legal documents setting out a child's support) in mainstream schools (£356k), 32 more at The Harbour School (£262k) and 68 more post-16 pupils at City of Portsmouth College (£173k). Placements with other local authorities are costing over 50% more than budgeted (£122k), and opening an inclusion centre adds £51k. A £546k underspend on the Early Years Inclusion Fund partly offsets this, because a planned centre is not opening and pupil numbers are lower than forecast.

Separately, the Department for Education cut early years funding by £1.0m in July after the January 2026 census. As in previous years, the council offset the cut against the carried-forward deficit, which reduced the balance available for high needs pressures. That raised the budgeted overspend from £537k to £1,525,200. The papers give a high needs funding shortfall of £7.527m and say the grant is ring-fenced, so its deficit cannot be offset against the council's general fund.
news_drafts.paper_title: Dedicated Schools Grant 2026/27 (Quarter 1) Budget Monitorig and Revised Budget

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 26-27 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: MUFG's central forecast has the Base Rate rising to 4.0% in the short term, then falling to 3.25% during 2028
findings.detail: The paper reports MUFG's central forecast, last updated after the September MPC meeting. It notes that some forecasters are suggesting a base rate of 4.75% by autumn 2027, and that PWLB rates are expected to decline gradually over one to three years, with significant upside risks.
findings.matters: The gap between the central forecast and some forecasters' 4.75% view affects how councils price new borrowing and refinancing over the next three years.
findings.figures: Central forecast Base Rate 4.0% short term, 3.25% during 2028; some forecasters 4.75% by autumn 2027
findings.quote: anticipates that the Base Rate will increase to 4.0% in the short term, before gradually reducing to 3.25% during 2028

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 26-27 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Base Rate held at 3.75% through the first half of 2026/27; a quarter-point rise on 5 November 2026 is described as 'highly likely'
findings.detail: The paper reports the MPC voted 6-3 to hold the Base Rate at 3.75% on 17 September 2026, with three members voting for an immediate increase to 4.0%. It says market expectations for a quarter-point rise at the 5 November 2026 meeting are 'highly likely', with further increases considered possible during 2027.
findings.matters: A higher Base Rate raises the cost of variable and refinancing debt and the yield on cash, so councils with similar exposure will read the expected rise as a direct change to their budgets.
findings.figures: Base Rate 3.75%; MPC vote 6-3 to hold; three members voted for 4.0%; expected rise a quarter percentage point
findings.quote: current market expectations indicate that a quarter percentage point increase in the Base Rate at the Monetary Policy Committee meeting on 5 November 2026 is highly likely

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 26-27 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: No breaches of the Treasury Management Policy in the second quarter of 2026/27
findings.detail: The paper states there were no breaches of the Treasury Management Policy in the second quarter of 2026/27. Gross borrowing of £707m sits within the authorised limit of £1,108m and the operational boundary of £1,084m.
findings.matters: Confirmation of policy compliance against approved prudential limits is the baseline assurance a finance director and a lender look for in a mid-year review.
findings.quote: There have been no breaches of these policies during this second quarter of financial year 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 26-27 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Net debt £507m, with net interest of £7.6m to 30 September 2026
findings.detail: The combined position shows £707m of borrowing, including finance leases and PFI schemes, at an average rate of 3.36%, with £11.9m of interest to 30 September 2026. Investments of £200m at an average of 4.34% produced £4.3m of interest.
findings.matters: Net debt and net interest are the figures a finance director compares across councils to show the cost of carrying debt against cash returns.
findings.figures: Borrowing £707m at 3.36%, interest £11.9m; investments £200m at 4.34%, interest £4.3m; net debt £507m; net interest £7.6m

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Mid-Year Review 26-27 with Appendix A Final
findings.headline: £90.6m, or 50.4% of the £180m invested at 30 September 2026, was placed with local authorities
findings.detail: Local authorities were the largest group in the investment portfolio, ahead of AAA-rated covered bonds at 19.3% and AAA-rated money market funds at 16.0%. The paper describes loans to local authorities as particularly attractive currently due to strong security, favourable yields and a range of maturities.
findings.matters: A council acting as a lender to other councils is a visible example of the inter-authority lending market, and its appetite for that lending affects pricing for other councils.
findings.figures: £90.6m (50.4%) with local authorities; £180m total invested; covered bonds £34.7m (19.3%); money market funds £28.8m (16.0%)
findings.quote: The three largest elements of the portfolio were invested in local authorities (£90.6m, 50.4%)

daily_post.headline: Interest rate outlook reversed; Base Rate cuts occurred earlier than forecast but further cuts are now unlikely with possible increases
daily_post.lead: A reversal from expected falling rates to potential rising rates affects both the council's future borrowing costs and investment income; this undermines the economic case for the current internal-borrowing strategy.
